subtype: Anxiety mistaken for laziness or attitude [Observer]
passage:
Vasudha, you called that student lazy just now. I said the same once, thirty years ago. There was a boy in my second-year class, Anil, bright in discussions, but he missed every essay deadline. When I reminded him, he snapped, "I'll do it, Disha Ma'am, stop chasing me." I wrote him off as careless and arrogant.
Then one evening I found him in the empty corridor, staring at a blank page, hands shaking. Instead of scolding, I asked, "What makes this so hard?" He was quiet for a long time. Then he said that every time he started, his chest went tight and he was sure it would be rubbish, so he stopped. It wasn't attitude. It was fear. The next day I walked him to the student counsellor, and we broke his essays into small pieces. He finished the year.

qa.q: What did Anil keep missing?
qa.a: Anil missed every essay deadline.

qa.q: What did Disha believe about Anil before that evening, and how did she feel?
qa.a: Disha felt irritated and believed Anil was careless and arrogant, because he missed deadlines and snapped at reminders.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Disha's story?
qa.a: Finding Anil with a blank page and shaking hands, Disha asked kindly what made it hard instead of scolding, which let him explain.

qa.q: What was the essay work like for Anil?
qa.a: For Anil, each start brought a tight chest and a certainty it would be rubbish, so he stopped out of fear, not laziness.

grounding: A teacher mistakes a student's missed deadlines and irritability for carelessness until asking kindly reveals anxiety and leads to support.

subtype: Anxiety mistaken for laziness or attitude [Observer]
passage:
With the group project due Thursday and the hostel Wi-Fi dropping every hour, Neelam had no patience left. Trisha had missed two meetings, left three messages unanswered and, when asked about her slides, snapped, "I said I'd do them!"
"She's just not bothered," Neelam told the others.
That night, during a power cut, Neelam found Trisha sitting on the dark stairwell, knees drawn up. Neelam almost walked past. Instead she sat down. "Are the slides feeling hard?"
"Every time I open the laptop, my heart starts hammering and I can't think," Trisha said. "I keep avoiding it, and then I hate myself."
"That sounds exhausting. I thought you didn't care."
"I care too much."
They split the slides into small parts by torchlight, and the next morning Trisha booked a slot with the college counsellor.

qa.q: Where did Neelam find Trisha during the power cut?
qa.a: Neelam found Trisha sitting on the dark stairwell.

qa.q: What did Neelam feel about Trisha before the stairwell?
qa.a: Neelam felt impatient and annoyed, believing Trisha was just not bothered.

qa.q: What did Neelam do on the stairwell that changed things?
qa.a: Neelam sat down and asked kindly whether the slides felt hard, which let Trisha explain, and then they split the work into small parts.

qa.q: How was Trisha experiencing the project?
qa.a: For Trisha, opening the laptop set her heart hammering, so she avoided it and then hated herself, because she cared too much.

grounding: A groupmate reads missed meetings and irritability as carelessness until a kind question reveals anxiety and leads to support.

subtype: Anxiety mistaken for laziness or attitude [Observer]
passage: By the fifth missed deadline, Chandrika had written Dilnaz off. The second-year student came late, snapped at her project partner, and hadn't submitted a single lab report since August. 'Attitude problem,' another lecturer said in the staffroom. But Chandrika kept seeing small things: Dilnaz's hands shaking when she was called on, the way she sat nearest the door. After class she asked Dilnaz to stay. 'I'm not calling you in to scold. I've noticed things seem hard lately. What's going on?' Dilnaz stared at the desk. Then it spilled out: she opened the portal every night, felt her chest tighten and shut the laptop, over and over, and then hated herself for it. 'I'm not lazy, ma'am. I just freeze.' Chandrika walked her to the student counsellor's office that afternoon and agreed a new timetable for the reports.

qa.q: At which missed deadline had Chandrika written Dilnaz off?
qa.a: By the fifth missed deadline.

qa.q: What did Chandrika feel as she noticed Dilnaz's shaking hands?
qa.a: Chandrika felt uneasy and concerned, sensing that something other than attitude might be going on.

qa.q: What made Chandrika's approach work?
qa.a: She asked kindly what was hard instead of scolding, then took Dilnaz to the counsellor and set a new timetable.

qa.q: What is it like for Dilnaz to be called lazy?
qa.a: It adds shame to her fear, since she already hates herself for freezing each night.

grounding: Shows a lecturer who first reads missed deadlines and irritability as carelessness, then notices the signs of anxiety and asks kindly, letting the student explain and find support.

'Sharmila skipped the presentation again. That's three times. I'm done covering for her.'
Nilesh put his bag down. 'Maybe. But did you see her hands in the library? She was shaking.'
'She was annoyed because I asked for her slides.'
'She snapped at me too. But Arun, she stood outside the seminar room last week. Just stood there. Then walked off.'
'So?'
'So I don't think it's laziness.'
That evening Nilesh found Sharmila on the hostel steps. 'Hey. Not here to fight. You okay? Presentations seem really hard for you.'
She looked away. 'I get this tight chest. My voice disappears. I'd rather take a zero than stand up there.'
'That sounds awful. Would it help to talk to the counselling centre? I can walk over with you tomorrow.'
'Maybe.' Then, quietly: 'Thanks for asking instead of shouting.'

qa.q: How many times had Sharmila skipped the presentation?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What made Nilesh doubt it was laziness?
qa.a: He felt uneasy after seeing her shaking hands and her standing outside the seminar room, then walking off, which looked like fear.

qa.q: What small step helped Sharmila open up?
qa.a: Nilesh approached her calmly, said he was not there to fight and asked if presentations were hard for her.

qa.q: How does Sharmila see the zeros she has been taking?
qa.a: To her, a zero feels easier than the tight chest and vanishing voice of standing up to present.

grounding: Shows a classmate who notices that missed presentations and snapping may be anxiety, not laziness, and asks kindly so the student can explain and find support.

subtype: Anxiety mistaken for laziness or attitude [Observer]
passage: For most of our first year, I thought Sabina had an attitude. She'd cancel our study plans at the last minute, bite my head off if I asked about assignments, and once missed a whole exam she'd told me she'd prepared for. I'm Sunaina, and I'll admit I complained about her to our other roommate more than once. Then one night I heard her in the bathroom, breathing like she'd been running. When she came out, I didn't make a joke. I just asked, 'Is something hard right now?' She sat on my bed and said her chest went tight every time she opened her books, and that avoiding them was the only thing that made it stop. She wasn't careless. She was scared. Next day I went with her to the college counsellor. She still has hard weeks, but she tells me now.

qa.q: Who did Sunaina complain to about Sabina?
qa.a: Their other roommate.

qa.q: What did Sunaina feel after hearing Sabina's breathing through the bathroom door?
qa.a: Sunaina felt worried and a little guilty, beginning to see that something more than attitude was going on.

qa.q: What could a friend in Sunaina's place try earlier?
qa.a: Ask gently what is hard, instead of complaining, as soon as the cancellations and snapping start.

qa.q: How did avoiding her books seem to feel for Sabina?
qa.a: It was the only thing that made her tight chest stop, even though it made things worse.

grounding: Shows a friend who first reads missed plans and irritability as attitude, then asks kindly and learns the student is anxious, helping her find support.

subtype: Anxiety mistaken for laziness or attitude [Observer]

Lecturer's note, second-year design, Wasim
Wasim has missed three submission deadlines and snapped at his group when they asked for his part. My first reading, I admit, was that he was careless. The group called him lazy. Before marking him down, I asked him to stay after class and asked, 'What's making this hard?' He was quiet, then said that every time he opens the file his chest tightens and he freezes, sure it won't be good enough, so he avoids it. That isn't laziness. We broke the next project into three small check-ins with me, and I told him about the student support centre. He booked an appointment before he left.
Divyansh

qa.q: How many deadlines has Wasim missed?
qa.a: Three submission deadlines.

qa.q: What did Divyansh first think, and how did that change?
qa.a: Divyansh first thought Wasim was careless, then felt concerned on hearing that the avoidance came from worry about not being good enough.

qa.q: What support did Divyansh offer?
qa.a: Breaking the project into three small check-ins and pointing Wasim to the student support centre.

qa.q: How might Wasim feel when asked 'What's making this hard?'
qa.a: He may have felt relieved to be asked kindly rather than judged, which let him explain.

grounding: A lecturer nearly reads a student's avoidance and irritability as carelessness, then asks kindly and finds anxiety behind it.
